prompt: How many 2.4 GHz channels can networks in range of each other use without overlapping?
hint: The numbers are 5 MHz apart; the signals are not 5 MHz wide.

choices.text: Thirteen, one per number in the menu
choices.why: Each signal covers about five numbers, so neighbours in the menu overlap.

choices.text: Three: 1, 6 and 11
choices.why: Right. 25 MHz apart, more than the 22 each one needs.

choices.text: Seven, the odd numbers from 1 to 13
choices.why: Odd numbers are 10 MHz apart, and a signal is 20 or 22 MHz wide.

choices.text: Eleven, in countries that stop at channel 11
choices.why: Where the band stops matters little; overlap is about spacing.

prompt: What is the centre frequency of 2.4 GHz channel 6, in MHz?
Channels 1 and 6 both look busy, so a new network is put on channel 3. What did that achieve?
hint: Where does a channel 3 signal spread?

choices.text: A free channel of its own between the two
choices.why: Channel 3 spreads over 1 to 5: it is not between them, it is on top of both.

choices.text: It shares airtime with channel 1 and leaves 6 alone
choices.why: It overlaps both, and it cannot decode either, so it shares nothing politely.

choices.text: Interference from and to the networks on 1 and 6
choices.why: Right. It overlaps both and can decode neither, which is worse than sharing channel 1.

choices.text: Nothing, as channel numbers are just labels
choices.why: A number is the address of a frequency; channel 3 is 2422 MHz.

prompt: A channel number is the address of a signal's ___ frequency, 2412 MHz for channel 1.
An access point on channel 100 moves itself to channel 36 at noon, and every client reconnects. What is the likeliest reason?

choices.text: It heard radar, and DFS made it leave
choices.why: Right. Ten seconds to leave, thirty minutes before it may come back.

choices.text: A neighbour took channel 100 and pushed it off
choices.why: Wi-Fi networks share a channel; none can push another off.

choices.text: Its firmware crashed and it restarted
choices.why: A restart would bring it back on its configured channel, not a different one.

choices.text: Channel 100 is licensed only in the mornings
choices.why: No channel has hours; the move follows a detection.

prompt: Outside the weather-radar channels, how many seconds does an access point listen, silent, before it may transmit on a DFS channel?
Put the life of an access point on a DFS channel in order.
items: It starts sending beacons and serving clients
It stops and moves its clients within 10 seconds
It stays off that channel for 30 minutes
trap: The check comes before the first beacon: an access point on a radar channel is invisible for its first minute.

prompt: A hospital's voice handsets must never lose their network in the middle of a call. Which 5 GHz channels should that network use?
hint: Which channels can be taken away?

choices.text: UNII-2C, for its twelve channels
choices.why: Twelve channels, all of which radar can take away with ten seconds' notice.

choices.text: All twenty-five, to have the most choice
choices.why: Sixteen of them are radar channels, and a move drops every call.

choices.text: Only UNII-1 and UNII-3: channels 36 to 48 and 149 to 165
choices.why: Right. The nine channels radar never takes.

choices.text: The DFS channels, which radar keeps other networks off
choices.why: Radar keeps Wi-Fi off, including yours, at a moment nobody chooses.

prompt: Two access points in the same office hear each other on channel 1. Which change is worse than leaving them there?
hint: Same channel: they decode each other.

choices.text: Moving one of them to channel 6
choices.why: 6 does not overlap 1, so that is an improvement.

choices.text: Moving one of them to channel 3
choices.why: Right. On 3 they overlap and cannot decode each other, so they stop waiting and start corrupting.

choices.text: Moving one of them to channel 11
choices.why: 11 is clear of 1; that is an improvement too.

choices.text: Moving one of them to 5 GHz
choices.why: A different band does not overlap at all.

prompt: Match each situation to what a Wi-Fi radio does about it.
hint: Can it decode what it hears?

pairs.left: A neighbour's preamble on the same channel, at −80 dBm
A neighbour on an overlapping channel, at −70 dBm
pairs.right: It transmits over it: adjacent-channel interference

pairs.left: A microwave oven next to it, at −55 dBm
pairs.right: It waits, having heard only energy above −62 dBm

right_distractors: It leaves the channel within 10 seconds

prompt: Which of these disturb Wi-Fi on 2.4 GHz? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: A microwave oven while it runs
choices.why: Right: around 2450 MHz, leaking from the door.

choices.text: A room full of Bluetooth headsets
choices.why: Right: each hops over the band; together they add up.

choices.text: A DECT cordless phone bought in Brazil
choices.why: DECT works near 1.9 GHz, outside every Wi-Fi band.

choices.text: A baby monitor on a fixed frequency
choices.why: Right: some transmit without a pause.

prompt: The Wi-Fi in a break room fails for a few minutes around noon every day, and nowhere else. The access point shows retries and noise, and no other network nearby. What will show the cause?

choices.text: A capture of the Wi-Fi frames at noon
choices.why: A capture holds frames, and the culprit sends none; you would see only the retries.

choices.text: The access point's list of neighbouring networks
choices.why: It is not a network, so it will never appear there.

choices.text: A spectrum analyser in the room at noon
choices.why: Right. It draws energy against frequency, and a microwave oven has a shape anybody recognises.

choices.text: A speed test run at noon
choices.why: It confirms the slowness, which nobody doubted, and names no cause.

prompt: The energy threshold, −62 dBm, is how many times more power than the preamble threshold, −82 dBm?
hint: Every 10 dB is a factor of ten.

prompt: How many milliwatts is 20 dBm?
hint: 0 dBm is 1 mW, and each 10 dB is ten times.

prompt: An access point's power goes from 17 dBm to 20 dBm. What happened to its power in milliwatts?

choices.text: It went up by 3 mW
choices.why: A decibel is a ratio, not an amount: +3 dB is a factor.

choices.text: It went up by about 18%, 3 on 17
choices.why: That treats a logarithmic scale as a linear one.

choices.text: It doubled, to twice the milliwatts
choices.why: Right. +3 dB is twice the power: about 50 mW became 100 mW.

choices.text: It tripled, 3 dB for three times
choices.why: A factor of three is about 4.8 dB; 3 dB is a factor of two.

prompt: A radio puts out 20 dBm into a cable that loses 1 dB, feeding an antenna with 6 dBi of gain. What is the EIRP, in dBm?
hint: Gains and losses in dB simply add.

prompt: One laptop reports −50 dBm and another −70 dBm from the same access point. Which receives more power, and by how much?
hint: 20 dB is two factors of ten.

choices.text: The one at −70 dBm, because 70 is the larger number
choices.why: The minus sign reverses it: closer to zero is stronger.

choices.text: The one at −50 dBm, by about 40%
choices.why: That reads 20 on 50 as a linear difference; dB are ratios.

choices.text: The one at −50 dBm, by twice the power
choices.why: Twice is 3 dB. These are 20 dB apart.

choices.text: The one at −50 dBm, a hundred times more
choices.why: Right. 20 dB is 10 × 10.

prompt: At the far end of an office, a phone shows good bars, and pages barely load. The access point is set to maximum power. What is the likeliest explanation?

choices.text: The bars are wrong and the signal is weak
choices.why: The bars are right about the direction they measure, the access point to the phone.

choices.text: Its replies arrive too weak
choices.why: Right. The access point is louder than the phone, and the uplink is the weak half.

choices.text: The access point should go higher still
choices.why: That strengthens the direction that already works.

choices.text: The phone's antenna is faulty
choices.why: It hears perfectly well. Nothing needs to be broken for this to happen.

prompt: An access point transmits at 23 dBm and a phone at 14 dBm, with 100 dB of path loss between them in both directions. At what level does the access point hear the phone, in dBm?
A dense office runs every 2.4 GHz access point at maximum power. What does turning them all down to about the phones' level do?

choices.text: Creates dead spots and gains nothing else
choices.why: With access points placed for it, the cells still cover; what shrinks is the overlap.

choices.text: Smaller cells, less channel sharing, honest bars
choices.why: Right. Fewer access points hear each other on the same channel, and each link is as good up as down.

choices.text: Faster rates for each client, as the noise in the room falls
choices.why: A client far from its access point gets a weaker signal; the gain is in contention and roaming.

choices.text: Nothing measurable, since power affects only the bars on screen
choices.why: Power decides who hears whom, which is what contention is made of.

prompt: Order these received levels from the strongest to the weakest.
trap: The minus sign reverses the order of the digits: −90 dBm is a million times weaker than −30.

prompt: The rules that make a 5 GHz access point check for radar, and leave a channel when it hears some, are called ___.
To fix slow uploads from phones in a far room, a consultant raises the access point's transmit power from 17 to 23 dBm. What changes?

choices.text: Uploads arrive 6 dB stronger too
choices.why: The phone's power did not change, so neither did what the access point hears.

choices.text: Uploads become four times as fast, like the power
choices.why: The fourfold power went into the downlink only.

choices.text: Stronger bars on screen, and no faster sending
choices.why: Right. The weak half was phone to access point, and that did not move.

choices.text: Nothing at all changes, on the phones or on the access point
choices.why: The downlink does get 6 dB stronger; it was not the problem.
